title: Reporting and quarantining suspicious mail
body_md:
## Report the message without spreading it

Recognizing a suspicious email is useful; getting it to the right review channel may help others. A report is **not** a guarantee that a campaign will be blocked, that money will be recovered, or that every copy will disappear. Treat reporting as part of a calm response, followed by any account or payment action your actual exposure requires.

### Choose the recipient

For personal mail, use your provider's built-in phishing report when available. In Gmail on a computer, open the message menu beside Reply and choose **Report phishing**. Google says a manually reported message, including attachments, may be copied and analyzed for abuse protection. Outlook.com has **Report → Report phishing**; Microsoft notes that reporting a sender does not itself block future messages from that sender. Menu names and locations can change.

For workplace or school mail, use the organization's security-report button or the channel in its policy. Preserve the message until its team tells you how to handle it; some teams want the original as an attachment so headers survive. Do not send a live suspicious email to a wide colleague list. A screenshot may help discussion, but the security team may need the original message for analysis.

In the UK, the NCSC asks people to forward doubtful emails to report@phishing.gov.uk. In the US, the FTC describes reporting to ReportFraud.ftc.gov and forwarding phishing email to the Anti-Phishing Working Group. These are jurisdiction-specific options, not a single worldwide mailbox. Check official current instructions before sending a report, especially if the message contains private workplace or customer information.

### Then contain what happened

Do not reply, open an attachment or use the unsubscribe link in a message you suspect is malicious. A legitimate subscription you chose is different: use the provider's normal unsubscribe controls or account preferences. After reporting, follow your provider's or organization's instructions for moving to Junk, retaining or deleting the message; there is no universal “keep it in quarantine” rule. If you clicked, downloaded, entered credentials or paid, tell support what happened and take the relevant recovery steps promptly through independently found channels. Do not hide a mistake out of embarrassment.

The goal is an accurate signal to the right place, with minimum extra exposure. You can say “I am not sure” in a report. Suspicion is enough to ask for a review.

widget_config.goal: Route a suspicious email to the appropriate provider or organization and describe any interaction honestly.
widget_config.today_action: Find the phishing-report control or internal security contact for one mail account you use. Note the route without sending a real message for this exercise.
widget_config.scope: Gmail and Outlook steps apply to named products as checked on 20 October 2026; UK NCSC and US FTC routes are local. Workplace policy and privacy rules take priority.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: fake staff rota
blocks.situation: A message to several employees claims a new rota is attached. The sender name resembles HR, but the request was not announced and the file is unexpected. One colleague asks you to forward it.
blocks.analysis: Do not open or widely forward the file. Use the workplace report channel and describe the claimed sender, attachment and recipients. Ask HR through the known internal directory whether a rota was sent. Let security decide retention and containment.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: wanted newsletter in Junk
blocks.situation: A newsletter you subscribed to appears in Junk after a platform migration. Its topic and sender are familiar, but the delivery address changed.
blocks.analysis: A changed address can be legitimate. Check your subscription in the publisher's normal account or official site. If confirmed, use the mail client's 'not spam' control; do not report it as phishing solely because it reached Junk. If it asks for a surprising password or payment, verify separately.

blocks.title: The shared mailbox warning
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise. A team mailbox receives a supposed file-sharing alert; no real message or attachment is used.

steps.prompt: The alert asks everyone to open an attachment. You have not interacted. What first?

choices.text: Leave the attachment closed and use the team's report channel.
choices.consequence: Security receives the original through the expected route.
choices.explanation: Reporting can start without opening the file.

choices.text: Forward the entire message to all teammates as a warning.
choices.consequence: The active attachment reaches more people.
choices.explanation: A wide forward spreads the payload.

steps.prompt: The report form asks whether anyone clicked. You clicked the message but not the file. What do you write?

choices.text: State exactly that you viewed the message but did not open the attachment.
choices.consequence: Responders can assess the actual exposure.
choices.explanation: Clear facts help more than a confident guess.

choices.consequence: Responders receive an inaccurate incident description.
choices.explanation: Distinguish viewing a message from opening its link or file.

steps.prompt: A coworker says they entered a password after following the link. What advice?

choices.text: Wait for security to prove compromise first.
choices.consequence: Recovery may be delayed while access is at risk.
choices.explanation: Potential credential disclosure needs prompt action.

choices.text: Tell them to contact security and change the password through the real service, following its guidance.
choices.consequence: The exposure and response reach the right team.
choices.explanation: Include any code or approval in the report.

steps.prompt: Later, security acknowledges a report about this message. What do you do with your copy?

choices.text: Assume every recipient is protected and delete evidence regardless of policy.
choices.consequence: You may discard material the team needs.
choices.explanation: A report does not guarantee instant blocking.

choices.text: Follow the team's instruction for retaining, moving or deleting it.
choices.consequence: The evidence and mailbox are handled under the local procedure.

blocks.debrief: Good reporting is precise and routed correctly. It neither replaces recovery after exposure nor guarantees automatic protection. Retry the decisions that spread the mail or concealed details.

questions.prompt: Your workplace has a dedicated phishing-report button. A suspicious attachment arrives. What is best?

choices.text: Use that button without opening or mass-forwarding the attachment.
choices.explanation: The local security process receives the message.

choices.text: Forward it to every colleague so they can decide.

questions.prompt: A newsletter you requested lands in Junk. Is that proof of phishing?

choices.text: No; verify the subscription separately and correct the classification if genuine.
choices.explanation: A confusing legitimate case needs a check, not an automatic accusation.

questions.prompt: You reported a suspicious Outlook.com sender. What is safe to assume?

choices.text: The report is submitted, but the sender is not necessarily blocked.
choices.explanation: Microsoft explicitly separates reporting and blocking.

choices.text: Every future email from that sender is blocked for everyone.
choices.explanation: The report does not promise that outcome.

questions.prompt: You entered a password through a suspected phishing link. Is reporting the email enough?

choices.text: Yes; a report automatically restores the account.
choices.explanation: Reporting and account recovery are separate.

choices.text: No; report what happened and change the password through the real service, seeking support.
choices.explanation: Respond to the actual exposure promptly.
